about.title: Bakersfield Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: A work injury in Bakersfield rarely stays at work. It follows you home, into the bills, and into the question of who actually pays. In Kern County, the answer usually starts with workers' compensation: your employer's insurer covers medical care and part of your lost wages no matter who was at fault, and that benefit is normally the only claim you can bring against the employer itself. What many people don't hear is that a separate claim may exist when someone outside your company caused the harm. Picture a delivery driver rear-ended on Panama Lane during the Friday 5 p.m. rush, a laborer hurt by a subcontractor's shortcut, or a machine that failed because it was built wrong. Those are third-party cases, and they carry their own two-year deadline. Bakersfield recorded 1,436 injury collisions in 2025 with 2,245 people hurt, and anyone injured while driving for work faces both systems at once. LawProactive is not a law firm. We simply connect you, free, with an independent attorney who can sort out which paths are open to you.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines and Your Job Protection
items.desc: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, and it is illegal for an employer to retaliate against you for doing so. An attorney can help you document the report and respond if pushback follows.

items.title: Free to Connect, Contingency to Hire

items.question: I was hit on Union Avenue while making deliveries for my employer. Is that a workers' comp case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It can be both. Because you were on the clock, workers' compensation should cover your medical treatment and part of your wages no matter who caused the crash. If the other driver was at fault, you may also have a separate third-party claim against that driver, and that claim follows the two-year deadline that applies to ordinary injury cases. Bakersfield saw 1,436 injury collisions in 2025, many along corridors like Union Avenue, White Lane, and Ming Avenue, so this overlap comes up more often than people expect.

items.question: Can my employer punish me for reporting a workplace injury?
items.answer: No. Retaliating against a worker for reporting an injury or filing a workers' compensation claim is illegal in California. You should still report the injury to your employer within 30 days so your claim is not delayed. If you notice reduced hours, demotion, or termination after reporting, tell the attorney you are connected with right away.

items.question: Why would I need an attorney if workers' comp already covers me?
items.answer: Workers' comp is limited by design and does not pay for things like pain and suffering, and it generally blocks you from suing your employer. An attorney can check whether a third party such as a subcontractor, property owner, or equipment manufacturer contributed to your injury, which could support an additional claim. Coordinating the two so one does not undercut the other is where independent legal guidance matters most.
